steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Evaluation means assessing what worked, what didn't, and why — it is the most important part of citizenship action and worth the most marks in the exam.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Evaluate by comparing outcomes against original aims: Did you achieve what you set out to do? How do you know? What evidence supports your assessment?

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Consider both intended outcomes (what you planned) and unintended outcomes (unexpected results, positive or negative).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Use quantitative evidence (numbers: petition signatures, survey responses, attendance figures) and qualitative evidence (quotes, testimonials, observations, feedback).

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: Why is evaluation important in citizenship action? | Q: What is the difference between quantitative and qualitative evidence in evaluation? | Q: How should you structure an evaluation of your citizenship action?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Evaluation is important because it assesses whether the action achieved its aims, identifies what worked and what didn't, provides evidence of impact, and helps improve future actions. In the AQA exam | Quantitative evidence is numerical — e.g. 250 signatures collected, 80% of students supported the campaign. Qualitative evidence is descriptive — e.g. quotes from stakeholders about changing attitudes | Restate your original aims, assess whether each aim was met using evidence, discuss which methods worked well and why, identify what didn't work and analyse reasons, explain what you would do differen

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: AQA Paper 2 Section B is worth 24 marks — most marks are for evaluation, not description Always use specific evidence from your action, not vague generalisations Honest reflection scores higher than exaggerated claims of success
